catalog_quote: The tone system of Ts’amakko is based on a high tone and a low tone and has limited function load. It is not the case to make a full explanation of it in the present paper, as it suffices to state that, with some exception, tone is not marked in the Grammar of Ts’amakko. This is because the grammar provides information about the tonal characteristics of almost all word classes and verb paradigms and tone placement can be predicted from this information. An exception are those nominals that do not follow the default patterns HL or HHL. In these cases, tone is marked. The graphic rendering of tone is acute accent <´> for high tone and grave accent <`> for low tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Quote check: (28 pp., text; extracted text of p.7 = printed p.180) carries §2.1.3 'TONE' exactly as quoted, word for word ('The tone system of Ts'amakko is based on a high tone and a low tone and has limited function load.. tone placement can be predicted from this information. An exception are those nominals that do not follow the default patterns HL or HHL. In these cases, tone is marked.'), followed by 'The graphic rendering of tone is acute accent for high tone and grave accent for low tone.' I read the surrounding sections: §2.1.1-2.1.2 are segmental (consonants, five short/long vowels, lengthening before =ma), §2.1.4 is the transcription alphabet; nothing else on prosody for Ts'amakko…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Ts'amakko prominence is described as tone (H vs L), not stress: a restricted two-level system with low functional load whose placement is predictable from word class and verb paradigm; nominals by default carry H on the non-final syllable(s) and L on the final syllable (HL, HHL), with lexical exceptions marked; verbs get their tone pattern from the paradigm. No statement about stress as such.
new_statements.exceptions: Nominals that do not follow the default HL / HHL patterns are tone-marked in the grammar (acute = H, grave = L); 'with some exception' tone is otherwise unmarked because predictable.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level (citation-form nominals and verb paradigms) as transcribed in Savà's 2005 grammar; the author is summarising his own grammar's analysis. The full analysis (tone vs. pitch accent, pp. c. 28-35 of Savà 2005) was not accessible, so whether Savà labels it 'pitch accent' or 'tone' there is unverified; the 2021 text uses 'tone'. Reading 'pitch accent' chosen because placement is predictable/culminative-like (Cushitic restricted-tone type); 'tone language, no stress statement' would be the literal alternative.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Ts'amakko (self-name; = Tsamai/Tsamay/S'aamakko, ISO tsb, glottocode tsam1247), the Dullay variety spoken west of the Weyt'o river; Savà's data are from fieldwork for his 2005 Leiden grammar. The AMS 1980 excerpt concerns other Dullay varieties (Harso-Dobase, Gollango; cf. gaww1239/dullay), not Tsamai.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Savà 2021 statement that Ts'amakko is a two-tone (H/L) language with a low functional load and predictable placement; it adds one detail — a morphologically conditioned accent shift to the final syllable (plus first-syllable lengthening) under the clitic =ma — and does not state a default word-level placement. It does not contradict the catalog's tone-language reading. Copy obtained from the Internet Archive snapshot (2026-09-17 17:06Z) of the Leiden repository file, because scholarlypublications.universiteitleiden.nl serves an F5 bot-challenge page by automated download (two attempts saved as and leiden_item3158776_download.bin).
new_statements.rule_in_words: The article is about case morphology and has no phonology or prosody section; its examples carry no tone or accent marks. The one prosodic remark is morphophonological: when the destination clitic =ma attaches to a noun, the host's first-syllable vowel is lengthened and the word's 'accent' (in Savà's framework the H-tone/tonal accent of the Ts'amakko two-tone system) shifts to the host's last syllable. This presupposes that the accent normally sits elsewhere (non-final) on the bare noun, but the chapter does not state the default position. Fn. 4 (p. 168) adds that when =ta would be doubled, the possessor is marked instead by 'lengthening on the first syllable vowel'.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the clitic-triggered shift itself: =ma lengthens the host's first syllable and moves the accent to the host's final syllable; no other exceptions or default rule given.
new_statements.identity_note: Savà 2020 describes Ts'amakko (Bago Ts'amakkilo), the lowland Dullay variety west of the Weyt'o River in South Omo Zone — the same variety as the 2005 grammar and the catalog entry; no dialect split is mentioned.

tone_statements.citation: Savà, Graziano (2005). A Grammar of Ts'amakko. Cologne: Rüdiger Köppe. Rijksuniversiteit te Leiden. 296 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Two tones, High tone and Low tone, are distinguished in Ts’amakko. Tone is associated with the short or long syllable vowel. [...] On long vowels, high tone appears as a continued high pitch and low tone appears as a continued low pitch along the vowel. (p. 41, §2.4.1) | The Ts’amakko tonal system is functionally restricted. The following facts characterise the use of tone: - Two, or more, High tones must be part of a single string. - Tone is lexically determined in nominals and in verbs. - The vast majority of nominals show low tone on the final syllable and high tone on the preceding syllable(s). Other distributions of tone are exceptional. - Basic nouns are never distinguished only by tone. (p. 42, §2.4.2) | The distribution of high-pitched syllable vowels in Ts’amakko is best accounted for in the context of a tonal system. However, as it happens in the Cushitic languages, the Ts’amakko tonal system shows accentual features. There is a tendency to create one prominency in the attribution of one high pitch to the word.
